text:
Training many different machine learning models and averaging their predictions can improve performance [P3_p1_c02]. However, using a whole group of models together is cumbersome and can be too computationally expensive to deploy to a large number of users [P3_p1_c02]. 

This paper solves that problem by showing how to compress the knowledge from a group of models into a single, smaller model [P3_p1_c02][P3_p1_c04]. The main idea is a technique called distillation [P3_p2_c04]. This involves training the smaller model to match the outputs of the larger, cumbersome model [P3_p2_c04][P3_p2_c05]. 

Regarding results, the paper achieves surprising outcomes on MNIST [P3_p1_c02]. It also shows that distillation can significantly improve the acoustic model of a heavily used commercial system [P3_p1_c02]. 

Additionally, the paper introduces a new type of ensemble made of full models and specialist models [P3_p1_c02]. These specialist models learn to distinguish fine-grained classes that the full models confuse [P3_p1_c02]. Unlike a mixture of experts, these specialist models can be trained rapidly and in parallel [P3_p1_c02]. 

The sources do not provide specific metrics or data regarding cost, speed, or accuracy improvements beyond noting the significant improvement on the commercial system and the surprising results on MNIST [P3_p1_c02].
